pr_title: Clean up dangling S3 multipart uploads
pr_body:
If Elasticsearch fails part-way through a multipart upload to S3 it will
generally try and abort the upload, but it's possible that the abort
attempt also fails. In this case the upload becomes _dangling_. Dangling
uploads consume storage space, and therefore cost money, until they are
eventually aborted.

Earlier versions of Elasticsearch require users to check for dangling
multipart uploads, and to manually abort any that they find. This commit
introduces a cleanup process which aborts all dangling uploads on each
snapshot delete instead.

Closes #44971
Closes #101169

issue_context.title: Automatic cleanup of dangling multipart uploads
issue_context.body:
Today if a node fails part-way through a multi-part upload to a Cloud repository as part of a shard snapshot then Elasticsearch takes no action to clean it up. Instead we [push this responsibility onto users](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/repository-s3.html#_cleaning_up_multi_part_uploads) in the docs. Dangling multi-part uploads retain data and therefore cost money until they are cleaned up, and yet few users take note of this section of the docs.

For much of the time it would not be safe for Elasticsearch to clean up ongoing multi-part uploads since they may relate to a concurrently-running snapshot operation, but there are some occasions where such a cleanup would be safe. In particular, during snapshot deletion (and repository cleanup) we can be sure that there are no ongoing shard snapshots, and therefore all ongoing multipart uploads must be dangling or otherwise invalid and can be safely cancelled.

In theory we could also check for dangling multipart uploads when a snapshot completes and there are no more repository operations to perform, but in practice this'd be a little trickier to implement since we would need to block new snapshots from starting while the cleanup runs and today there is no mechanism to do that. I think this isn't necessary, snapshot deletions occur frequently enough to solve this.

review_comments: Does this mean that failures happening while getting list of multipart uploads would also fail the snapshot deletion? `getMultipartUploadCleanupListener` doesn't seem to throw. Sorry if this is not related, `ActionListener<ActionListener<>>` is really bumping this up to a whole new level! :)))

> Does this mean that failures happening while getting list of multipart uploads would also fail the snapshot deletion? Hm that was how it worked in an earlier iteration but in the finished version we log a failure there but otherwise treat it as if there are no multipart uploads. Let me try and simplify that, sec. > `ActionListener>` is really bumping this up to a whole new level

> Let me try and simplify that, sec.

Actually this is a little tricky, in principle we could turn this into a `Consumer<ActionListener<Void>>` but then we submit a task to a threadpool executor and that sort of thing can theoretically fail. It won't actually fail today because `snapshotExecutor` has an infinite queue and just silently drops work when shut down rather than rejecting it, but still I would prefer to write code like this in a style that allows for failures.

I'm ok with the `ActionListener<ActionListener<>>` part. FWIW, probably returning a specialized object with more clear names might make it more readable in my opinion, but that would anyway underneath be an action listener. But why log and propagate the failure if it's not supposed to happen?

If we're wrong (e.g. some future change to threadpool behaviour makes us wrong) then we have to do _something_ in production when assertions are disabled, this seems like the most sensible thing to do. There's loads of other spots where we `assert false` to indicate to the reader that we think something is impossible, but nonetheless react  in a somewhat reasonable fashion when assertions are disabled.
